name: Tomas Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play hand drums for a small community theatre, record simple rhythm cues and teach two beginners at a rehearsal centre. I finished secondary school and took up paid music after years as a hotel porter; at 58 I still ask the bandleader to check a hard cue. I like the moment an actor finds the beat without looking down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the household rely on from that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works regular hours at a library, and our children are grown with homes of their own. We rent a flat and have three months of expenses saved. The music pays about what this job usually does and there are some similar local posts, but I cannot assume a vacancy or a retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that faster call sheets are welcome if my paid cue and show time stay written down. The actor still needs a real beat when a scene runs late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months saved and my partner’s regular library wage cover a late cue fee. I want the next season signed, but this mild AI change does not threaten the work already booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid Saturday shows, two pupils and recorded cues this season. I use AI now and then for call times, checking against the stage manager’s sheet; before the next season I would ask for a written cancellation fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the household in this picture. We can carry one missed payment while the booked shows continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was a show cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall had a leak last spring and paid us for rehearsal but not the show. A written half-fee term would help us plan instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you teach a beginner first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask them to hear four even beats before a fill. Fast hands cannot rescue a beginner drum rhythm nobody can follow.

I would say actors still need a **real beat** when scenes run late.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and partner wage cover one delayed cue fee.
The **booked shows** still need signed terms, but AI adds little here.
do: Keep **paid Saturday shows**, two pupils and cues this season.
Request a **written half-fee term** before next season.
feel: I feel **calm** because current bookings and savings cover one delay.
S0.quote: Fast hands cannot rescue a beginner drum rhythm nobody can follow.
fieldNote: His **late-entry junior role** earns typical musician pay with three months saved and reliable household support from his partner.
Occasional **AI call sorting** is checked against the stage manager’s sheet.

steps.text: Keep paid Saturday theatre shows, two pupils and cue recordings this season
Request written half-fee cancellation term before next theatre season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that generated rhythm cues might remove small recording fees. I would ask the manager to put paid shows and revisions on one signed calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cues are about a quarter of my own pay, so fewer orders would be felt even with three months saved. I could still play live. An unsigned theatre season is not a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would request three months of paid calls and a paid sound-engineer demonstration of a new AI beat checker, which marks timing errors in a recorded drum cue. In the first year I would test it only on my own nameless take with the theatre’s licence and approved local storage, compare every mark against the original by ear, and stop if it shifts a beat or the file leaves the theatre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a cut to my own recording pay. I can learn a proven tool, but I still need the manager to buy a cue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload a pupil’s drum recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would use a take I own. A learner’s sound and name stay out of the trial without written consent and clear storage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the engineer offers an unpaid lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait for a paid demonstration and keep my paper timing marks. I will not lose a paid pupil hour for a free tool trial.

say: I would request **signed paid shows** and revision fees.
I would warn that **generated cues** could shrink recording work.
think: My **drum cues** supply about a quarter of my pay.
An **unsigned season** cannot replace lost recording income.
do: Request **three paid months** of theatre calls this month.
Test **beat checker** after paid engineer demo on owned nameless take with theatre licence/local storage; compare by ear and stop errors/leakage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost cue fees.
S1.quote: An unsigned theatre season is not a replacement wage.
fieldNote: The **new tool trial** needs paid instruction, a theatre licence, owned nameless sound and manual ear comparison.
Approved **local storage** and a timing/privacy stop protect the musician’s recording.

steps.text: Test beat checker after paid engineer demo on own nameless take, licensed/local storage; listen, stop errors/leakage
Keep paid shows and two pupils while requesting three months of signed calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that thinking AGI by 2028 could make the little drum cues cheaply. Robots able to play hand drums follow around 2031, three years later, so the cue invoice can disappear first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect cue orders to end in 2028, taking a quarter of my music pay. Some live calls might shrink, but three months saved and a few local theatres let us look before giving up a paid set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total cue invoices and ask for a signed paid theatre season. In the first year after 2028, if paid live calls fall too, I would apply for a posted arts-centre stage assistant job only if my secondary schooling and theatre experience qualify, written net pay after travel beats lost fees and the bus times work; I would keep paid shows and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the expected cue loss, with savings and local options giving some control. I would be alarmed if the live season collapsed as well, but I do not expect that yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot decide to retire at 60 from a birthday alone. I would first ask what any pension actually pays and compare it with rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an assistant post real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted vacancy with written hours and pay. I would not leave the theatre for a manager’s friendly mention.

say: I would warn **2028 thinking AGI** can make little drum cues cheaply.
I would distinguish lost **cue invoices** from playing robots around 2031.
think: I expect **cue orders** to end in 2028, removing a quarter of my own music pay.
Live **theatre cuts** remain possible, not my forecast, while current paid calls still hold.
do: Count **cue invoices** and request a signed paid theatre season now.
Seek **posted stage work** after 2028 live cuts if secondary schooling/theatre experience qualify, after-travel net beats losses and buses fit.
Keep **shows and pupils** until signed offer; ask what actual pension income pays and compare it with rent.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected recording loss while live calls may hold.
S2.quote: I cannot decide to retire at 60 from a birthday alone.
fieldNote: The expected **2028 cue loss** removes a quarter of his pay before 2031 hand-drum robots.
A stage move needs **posted eligibility**, written net replacement pay, reachable buses and signed offer.

steps.text: Total cue invoices and request signed paid theatre season now
Seek posted stage role after live cuts if secondary schooling/theatre experience qualify and buses fit
Require written net after travel beating losses; keep shows/pupils until signed offer
Ask actual pension income and compare with rent before stopping paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that five years until AGI by 2031 gives me time to learn a paid sound role. Playing robots follow around 2034, after cue-making changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cues may stop by 2031, when I will be 63. A sound certificate could help me work backstage, but a free course cannot replace paid rehearsal hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would ask the local theatre workshop for an actual paid six-month sound-assistant training place only if tuition is funded and class hours do not replace paid Saturday shows without equal wages. In the first year after 2031, if cue orders stop and paid shows shrink, I would seek a posted stage-sound job only if the certificate qualifies me and written net pay after travel beats lost fees on a bus route I can work; I would keep paid shows and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until both training and a job pay. Five years of warning does not pay the rent during an unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run electrical cables alone afterward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would start under the theatre electrician. I would not handle live wiring without a signed safety check and their approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the training place pays less than a show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid theatre calls and wait for another intake. Funded sound training with lower weekly wages is still a loss.

say: I would use **five years** to learn a paid sound role.
I would distinguish **2031 thinking AGI** from playing robots around 2034.
think: The **cue income** may end by 2031 before 2034 playing robots.
A **certificate** helps only when training pays and posted work accepts it.
do: Take **funded sound training** only with real paid place and wages matching displaced shows.
Seek **posted sound work** after 2031 cue and show cuts only if qualified, written net after travel beats losses and buses fit.
Keep **paid shows and pupils** until signed offer; work under electrician until live-wiring safety approval.
feel: I feel **anxious** about fees while requiring paid training and a real job.
S3.quote: Funded sound training with lower weekly wages is still a loss.
fieldNote: Training needs a **real paid place**, funded tuition and no lower weekly earnings.
The new job needs **posted qualification**, written net pay, workable buses and supervised wiring until approval.

steps.text: Take funded sound training only with actual paid place and wages matching displaced Saturday shows
Seek certificate-qualified posted sound job if cues/shows fall; written replacement net after travel, buses fit
Keep paid shows and pupils until suitable signed sound offer arrives
Work under electrician; avoid live wiring until safety check and approval signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to ask what retirement actually pays. Playing robots come around 2039. A date does not settle our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need theatre and pupil fees. Three months saved gives us some room now, yet I cannot claim a pension amount before I see a statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension statement and save twenty percent of each extra paid Saturday show after rent, food and bus fares toward six months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid sets and pupils while booked, and run a separate four-week beginner rhythm class only after written room and hire terms, with six adults prepaying enough for room hire, safe inspected loan drums and my teaching and preparation; I would repeat it only while six paid places still cover those costs, written room terms hold and safe drums remain available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about distant stage work with current shows paid and three months saved. Retirement at 68 will not pay our rent unless the pension statement gives us enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra shows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then nothing goes into savings from that source. I would not use food money to make a goal look reached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only three people pay for the rhythm class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund them and keep my paid pupils. Three fees cannot cover the room or preparation.

say: I would use **ten years** to ask what retirement actually pays.
I would say **2039 playing robots** do not settle our rent.
think: At **68**, I may still need theatre and pupil fees.
Our **three-month reserve** helps now but does not promise a funded retirement.
do: Request **pension statement** and save 20% of extra paid shows after rent, food and buses toward six months.
Keep **paid sets/pupils**; start class only with written room, six prepayments covering room, inspected drums and teaching/preparation.
Renew **rhythm class** only while six fees cover costs and room/safe drums remain; refund all buyers below six.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant work while current pay continues.
S4.quote: Retirement at 68 will not pay our rent unless the pension statement gives us enough.
fieldNote: His **six-month goal** uses twenty percent of real extra show pay after essentials.
The **paid rhythm class** requires six adult prepayments covering room, safe drums and his teaching/preparation.

steps.text: Request actual pension statement; keep paid sets and pupils after 2036 while booked
Save 20% of extra paid Saturday shows after rent/food/bus toward six months
Secure written room terms before six prepay room, inspected drums and teaching/preparation

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue fees may end before a real backstage job appears. Signed theatre dates, a funded paid sound course if needed, and a posted role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a sound course pays the week I take it. A certificate on the wall cannot cover the rent on Friday.

headlineQuote: A certificate on the wall cannot cover the rent on Friday.
portrait: At **58**, Tomas is a junior hand drummer with secondary schooling, a partner, grown children and three months saved.
His **typical music pay** comes from theatre sets, cue recordings and two pupils, with some similar local jobs.
He uses **AI occasionally** for calls and tests a new beat checker only after paid engineer instruction on owned audio.
He treats **retirement** as a decision based on an actual statement and keeps paid work if the numbers fall short.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end cue fees before a real paid backstage role opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed theatre dates**, funded paid sound training and posted qualified work with written net replacement pay would help Tomas.
